module_title: Marketing and Selling in Your Community

lessons.title: Identifying Your First Customers: Neighbours, Shops, and Market Stalls
lessons.body:
Your first customers are right around you. Start with your neighbours. Go door to door with a small pack of tissues and a smile. Say, "I make quality tissues at a good price. Would you like to try a pack for 500 shillings?" If they buy, great. If not, ask what price they usually pay and where they buy. This gives you real information.

Next, visit small shops and kiosks in your area. These are your best partners. Shop owners buy in bulk and sell to many people. Introduce yourself and your product. Offer them a sample pack free. Ask if they would stock your tissues. A common deal: you give them 10 packs at 400 shillings each, they sell at 500 shillings. They make 100 shillings profit per pack. That's fair.

Market stalls are also good. Go to your local market early in the morning when vendors are setting up. Talk to stall owners who sell household goods. Show them your tissues and your price list. Many will agree to try a small order of 20 packs. If they sell well, they will order more.

Don't forget offices, salons, and restaurants. These places use tissues daily. Visit them with a sample and a price list. Offer a weekly delivery service. For example, a restaurant might need 50 packs per week. That's steady income for you.

Keep a notebook. Write down every person you talk to, what they said, and when to follow up. Follow up within three days. Building these first customers takes time, but once they trust you, they will buy again and again.

lessons.title: Using WhatsApp and Social Media to Promote Your Products
lessons.body:
WhatsApp is your most powerful free marketing tool. Start by creating a WhatsApp Business account. You can download the app for free. Set your profile picture to a clear photo of your tissues. Write a short description: "Quality tissues at wholesale prices. Free delivery in [your area]."

Next, save the phone numbers of everyone you know: friends, family, neighbours, church members. Create a broadcast list called "Tissue Customers." Send them a message with a photo of your product and prices. For example: "Soft 2-ply tissues, 10 packs for 4,000 shillings. Order today, get free delivery." Keep messages short and clear. Don't spam. Send once or twice a week.

Join local community WhatsApp groups. Many neighbourhoods have groups for buying and selling. Post your offer there. Be polite and respond quickly to questions. If someone asks for 5 packs, deliver them that day if possible. Good service spreads fast.

Use Facebook too. Create a page called "[Your Name] Tissues." Post photos of your products, your prices, and happy customers (with their permission). Join Facebook groups for your town or city. Post in those groups. You can also use Instagram if you have a smartphone. Take short videos showing how you make or pack the tissues. People love to see the process.

Remember to include your phone number in every post. Ask customers to send you a WhatsApp message to order. Save every customer's number. Send them a message when you have a special offer, like "Buy 20 packs, get 2 free." This keeps them coming back.

lessons.title: Building Relationships with Local Retailers and Wholesalers
lessons.body:
Retailers and wholesalers can buy large quantities from you. But first, you must build trust. Start by visiting shops that already sell tissues. Observe what brands they stock and their prices. Then introduce yourself to the owner. Be respectful and dress neatly. Say, "I make quality tissues locally. I can offer you a better price than your current supplier."

Offer a trial order. For example, give them 20 packs at 350 shillings each. They can sell at 500 shillings. That's 150 shillings profit per pack. If they sell well, they will order more. Always deliver on time. If you promise delivery on Monday, deliver on Monday. Reliability is key.

For wholesalers, you need to offer even lower prices. A wholesaler might buy 500 packs at a time. Offer them 300 shillings per pack. They will sell to retailers at 400 shillings. You make less per pack, but you sell many more. That's good business.

Keep records of every sale. Write down the date, quantity, and amount paid. Also note when they might need more. After one week, visit again and ask, "How did the tissues sell? Do you need more?" If they sold out, they will be happy to see you.

Offer incentives. For example, "Buy 100 packs, get 10 free." Or "Pay within 7 days and get a 5% discount." This encourages larger orders and timely payment. Always thank them for their business. A small gift at Christmas, like a free pack of tissues, goes a long way.

lessons.title: Participating in Local Markets and Trade Fairs
lessons.body:
Local markets and trade fairs are great places to sell directly to many people. Find out when your local market day is. In many African towns, market day is every 5 days or on weekends. Book a stall early. The cost might be 1,000 to 5,000 shillings for the day. That's a small investment for big returns.

Set up your stall to attract attention. Use a bright cloth or banner. Arrange your tissue packs neatly. Have a sign with your prices: "10 packs for 4,000 shillings." Offer a special market price, like "Buy 5 packs, get 1 free." People love a deal. Stand up and greet people as they pass. Smile and say, "Quality tissues, soft and strong. Try a free sample." Have small sample pieces to give away.

At trade fairs, you can meet potential bulk buyers. These are events where businesses showcase products. Look for fairs organized by your local government or chamber of commerce. Register as an exhibitor. Bring plenty of stock, business cards, and a price list. Collect contact details from everyone interested. Follow up within two days.

During the market, keep a record of what sells best. Maybe the 2-ply tissues are more popular than 1-ply. Note the prices people are willing to pay. After the market, calculate your profit. Did you cover your stall fee and transport? If yes, do it again next week.

Markets are also good for learning. Watch what other tissue sellers do. See their prices and packaging. You can improve your own product based on what you see. And you might meet a wholesaler who wants to buy from you regularly.

lessons.title: Offering Free Samples to Schools and Offices
lessons.body:
Schools and offices use a lot of tissues every day. They are excellent customers because they buy regularly. But they need to trust your product first. The best way to get their attention is to offer free samples.

Start with schools. Visit the school office and ask to see the head teacher or administrator. Introduce yourself and explain that you make quality tissues at a good price. Give them a free pack of 10 tissues. Say, "Please try these in your staff room for a week. If you like them, I can supply you every month." Follow up after one week. If they liked the tissues, they will order. A typical school might need 100 packs per month. That's a big order.

For offices, target the person who handles supplies, often the office manager or receptionist. Give them a free sample pack. Ask them to test it in the office. Offer a special price for bulk orders, like 350 shillings per pack for orders over 50 packs. Also offer free delivery to their office. That saves them time and money.

When you give samples, always leave your contact details. A simple business card or a handwritten note with your phone number is fine. Write the price for bulk orders on the card. For example: "Bulk price: 50+ packs at 350 shillings each. Call [your number]."

Don't give samples to everyone. Focus on places that will buy in large quantities. Keep a list of the schools and offices you visited. Note the date and the person you spoke to. Follow up every two weeks until they order. Once they become customers, they often stay for years.

lessons.title: Word-of-Mouth Marketing: Satisfied Customers Tell Others
lessons.body:
Word-of-mouth is the cheapest and most powerful marketing. When a customer is happy, they tell their friends, family, and neighbours. That brings you new customers for free. But it only works if you give excellent service and quality products.

First, make sure your tissues are good. They should be soft, strong, and not tear easily. If your tissues are poor quality, people will complain and you will lose business. So always check your product before selling. Use good raw materials and pack them neatly.

Second, give great customer service. Be polite and friendly. Deliver on time. If a customer orders 10 packs, deliver them the same day if possible. If you can't, call and explain. Never ignore a customer. Answer your phone when they call. Reply to WhatsApp messages quickly.

Third, ask for referrals. After a customer buys, say, "Thank you. If you know anyone who needs tissues, please tell them about me." You can also offer a small reward. For example, "If you bring me a new customer who buys 10 packs, I will give you 2 free packs." This encourages people to spread the word.

Fourth, use your current customers to advertise. Ask them to post a photo of your tissues on their WhatsApp status or Facebook. Offer a small discount for doing so. For example, "Post a photo and get 10% off your next order." That exposes your product to all their contacts.

Finally, always follow up. After a sale, send a message: "Thank you for your business. How are the tissues?" If they are happy, ask them to tell others. If they have a problem, fix it immediately. A customer whose problem is solved becomes your best promoter.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Marketing and Selling Tissues & Paper Products in Your Community

This practical reference lesson consolidates the six core lessons in this module into a working field guide. It is written for small and growing African tissue and paper businesses â from a single-person operation producing toilet rolls in a backyard workshop to a registered SME supplying napkins, kitchen towels, and facial tissues across a district. The focus is commercial: how to find buyers, keep them, and grow sales without expensive advertising.

In most African markets, tissue and paper products are fast-moving consumer goods (FMCGs) with low unit prices and high repeat purchase rates. That means volume, distribution, and trust matter more than branding. A customer who buys a 10-roll pack today will need another next week. Your marketing job is not to convince people to use tissue paper â most already do â but to convince them to buy yours, consistently, from a place that is convenient.

1. Identifying Your First Customers: Neighbours, Shops, and Market Stalls

Your first customers are almost always within walking distance. Start with a simple mapping exercise: list every household within 500 metres, every kiosk and duka, every salon, barbershop, restaurant, and market stall within 2 kilometres. These are your warm leads. Neighbours buy in small quantities but provide immediate cash flow and honest feedback. Kiosks and dukas buy in slightly larger quantities and give you shelf visibility. Market stalls give you access to high-footfall locations where tourists, commuters, and bulk buyers pass through.

Segment your prospects by purchase behaviour:

  • Households: buy 4â10 rolls weekly; price-sensitive; respond to convenience and trust.
  • Kiosks/dukas: buy 20â100 rolls weekly; need reliable restocking; margin-sensitive.
  • Salons, barbers, restaurants: buy napkins and facial tissues in bulk; value consistency and presentation.
  • Schools, offices, churches: buy in bulk monthly or termly; require invoices and reliable delivery.

2. Using WhatsApp and Social Media to Promote Your Products

WhatsApp is the single most effective low-cost marketing channel for tissue products in most African markets. It is free, personal, and trusted. Use it deliberately:

  • Business profile: Set up WhatsApp Business with your business name, address, catalogue, and operating hours. Add product photos with prices.
  • Broadcast lists: Group customers by type (retail, wholesale, institutional) and send weekly stock updates, not spam.
  • Status updates: Post daily photos of new stock, deliveries, and customer feedback. Status is seen by contacts without being intrusive.
  • Groups: Join local market and community groups, but contribute value before selling. Share hygiene tips, not just adverts.
  • Facebook Marketplace and Instagram: Useful for reaching offices, hotels, and higher-income households. Post clear photos, prices in local currency, and a phone number.

Keep messages short, use local languages where appropriate, and always include a call to action: "Order today, delivered tomorrow."

3. Building Relationships with Local Retailers and Wholesalers

Retailers and wholesalers are your distribution backbone. A single wholesaler can move more stock in a week than 50 households in a month. Approach them professionally:

  • Offer trade terms: wholesale price, minimum order quantity, and clear payment terms (cash on delivery or 7-day credit for trusted buyers).
  • Provide point-of-sale support: branded stickers, shelf talkers, or simple display stands. These increase visibility and sales.
  • Guarantee restocking: visit weekly or bi-weekly. Reliability beats price discounts.
  • Handle complaints fast: replace defective stock immediately. Reputation is your most valuable asset.

4. Participating in Local Markets and Trade Fairs

Physical markets and trade fairs remain powerful in African contexts because they combine product demonstration, sampling, and immediate sales. A well-run market stall can generate more revenue in one day than a week of social media posts.

Preparation is everything. Bring enough stock, a clean display, price signs in local currency, and a way to capture customer contacts (a simple notebook or WhatsApp QR code). Trade fairs â organised by chambers of commerce, local government, or NGOs â are ideal for meeting wholesalers, institutional buyers, and potential distributors.

Table 1: Average weekly sales by channel for a small tissue producer (illustrative, East Africa)
Channel Average weekly units sold Average unit price (USD) Weekly revenue (USD) Gross margin
Neighbours (direct) 120 0.35 42 35%
Kiosks / dukas 400 0.28 112 25%
Market stalls 600 0.30 180 30%
Wholesalers 1,500 0.22 330 18%
Institutions (schools/offices) 800 0.25 200 22%

Source: Illustrative figures based on TechnoServe, Small Business Sales Benchmarks for Consumer Goods in East Africa (2021), and author field estimates. Actual figures vary by country, product type, and season.

5. Offering Free Samples to Schools and Offices

Free sampling is a proven technique for converting institutional buyers. Schools, offices, clinics, and restaurants are high-volume, repeat-purchase customers. A single school contract can consume 500â2,000 rolls per term.

How to sample effectively:

  • Target decision-makers: approach the procurement officer, school bursar, or office administrator directly.
  • Provide a professional sample pack: include 2â4 rolls or a pack of napkins with your business card and price list.
  • Follow up within 48 hours: ask for feedback and propose a trial order at a discounted rate.
  • Document the outcome: track conversion rates so you know which institutions are worth pursuing.

Sampling costs money, so limit it to high-potential buyers. A sample given to a household rarely converts; a sample given to a school bursar often does.

6. Word-of-Mouth Marketing: Satisfied Customers Tell Others

Word-of-mouth is the cheapest and most credible marketing channel in African communities. It is also the most fragile â one bad batch or one rude delivery can undo months of goodwill. To build positive word-of-mouth:

  • Deliver on time, every time. Reliability is the number one driver of referrals in low-trust markets.
  • Maintain consistent quality. Tissue that tears easily or napkins that fall apart will not be recommended.
  • Ask for referrals directly. "If you know someone who needs tissue, please send them to us."
  • Reward loyal customers. A free roll for every 10 purchased, or a small discount for referrals, builds loyalty.
  • Respond to complaints publicly and professionally. How you handle a problem is more visible than how you handle success.
Table 2: Customer acquisition cost comparison by marketing method (small tissue business, Africa)
Marketing method Typical cost (USD) Reach Conversion rate Cost per new customer (USD)
Word-of-mouth / referrals 0 â 5 Lowâmedium High (30â50%) 0.10 â 0.50
WhatsApp Business 2 â 10 (data) Medium Medium (10â20%) 0.50 â 1.50
Market stall / trade fair 20 â 100 (stall fees, transport) High (footfall) Mediumâhigh (15â30%) 1.00 â 3.00
Free samples (institutions) 10 â 50 (product cost) Low (targeted) High (20â40%) 2.00 â 5.00
Facebook / Instagram ads 20 â 200 High Low (2â8%) 5.00 â 15.00

Source: Adapted from GSMA, The Mobile Economy: Sub-Saharan Africa 2023 (GSMA Intelligence, 2023), and Nielsen, Trust in Advertising Global Report (2021). Conversion rates are indicative and vary widely by market and product.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Product Quality and Hygiene Compliance

Tissue and paper products come into direct contact with human skin and mucosal surfaces. In many African countries, tissue paper is regulated under national standards (e.g., KEBS in Kenya, SON in Nigeria, SABS in South Africa). Selling non-compliant or contaminated products can cause skin irritation, infections, and legal liability. Always:

  • Use virgin or properly de-inked pulp that meets local health standards.
  • Avoid recycled paper containing inks, dyes, or chemicals not approved for food-contact or skin-contact use.
  • Store finished products off the floor, away from moisture, chemicals, and pests.
  • Label products with your business name, batch number, and contact details for traceability.
  • Never sell visibly soiled, damp, or discoloured stock â even at a discount.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Map your 2 km radius: list every household, kiosk, salon, restaurant, school, and office. These are your first prospects.
  2. Set up WhatsApp Business with a catalogue, prices, and operating hours. Post stock updates at least 3 times per week.
  3. Visit 5 retailers per week with a clear wholesale price list, sample pack, and restocking schedule.
  4. Book one market stall or trade fair per month. Bring enough stock, price signs, and a way to capture contacts.
  5. Sample 2â3 institutions per month (schools, offices, clinics). Follow up within 48 hours.
  6. Ask every satisfied customer for a referral. Reward referrals with a small discount or free product.
  7. Track your numbers weekly: units sold, revenue, new customers, repeat customers, and complaints.
  8. Never compromise on quality or hygiene. One bad batch can destroy years of word-of-mouth goodwill.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-scale Food Processing Enterprise Development (free PDF)
  • GSMA â The Mobile Economy: Sub-Saharan Africa (free report)
  • TechnoServe â Small Business Resources and Toolkits (free downloads)
  • ILO â Small Enterprise Development Resources (free guides)
  • UNIDO â Industrial Development Resources for SMEs (free publications)

This lesson is part of the rise AFRICA skills course "Tissues & Paper Products." For the full module, see the companion lessons on production, costing, and quality control.

quiz.q: What is the best first step to find your first customers?
options: C) Print flyers and throw them from a car
D) Wait for customers to come to you
quiz.explanation: Your neighbours are the easiest and most accessible first customers.

quiz.q: When approaching a shop owner, what should you offer first?
quiz.explanation: A free sample lets the shop owner test your product without risk.

quiz.q: What is a fair profit margin for a shop owner selling your tissues?
quiz.explanation: A 100 shilling profit per pack is reasonable and motivates the shop to stock your product.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a notebook when visiting potential customers?
options: B) To record who you talked to and follow up
quiz.explanation: Recording details helps you remember and follow up with each contact.

quiz.q: Which places use tissues daily and could be regular customers?
quiz.explanation: Offices, salons, and restaurants use tissues frequently and need regular supply.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do when setting up WhatsApp for business?
options: A) Send bulk messages to strangers
B) Create a WhatsApp Business account
quiz.explanation: A WhatsApp Business account gives you tools to promote and manage customers.

quiz.q: How often should you send promotional messages to your WhatsApp broadcast list?
options: B) Once or twice a week
quiz.explanation: Sending too often is spam; once or twice a week keeps customers interested without annoying them.

quiz.q: What should you include in every social media post about your tissues?
quiz.explanation: Including your phone number makes it easy for customers to contact you to order.

quiz.q: What is a good way to use Facebook to promote your tissues?
options: A) Create a page and join local buying/selling groups
B) Only post once a year
quiz.explanation: A Facebook page and local groups connect you with potential customers in your area.

quiz.q: Why should you save your customers' phone numbers?
options: A) To call them at midnight
B) To send them special offers and updates
quiz.explanation: Saved numbers let you send targeted promotions and keep customers coming back.

quiz.q: When approaching a retailer, what should you do first?
options: B) Observe what they stock and their prices
D) Offer a very high price
quiz.explanation: Understanding their current stock and prices helps you make a competitive offer.

quiz.q: What is a good trial order for a new retailer?
quiz.explanation: A small trial order lets the retailer test the product without much risk.

quiz.q: Why is reliability important when supplying retailers?
options: A) It builds trust and repeat orders
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Delivering on time builds trust, so retailers will continue to buy from you.

quiz.q: What incentive can you offer a wholesaler to buy in bulk?
options: A) A lower price per pack
quiz.explanation: Wholesalers expect a lower price per pack for buying large quantities.

quiz.q: How often should you follow up with a retailer after a trial order?
quiz.explanation: Following up after a week lets you see if they sold out and need more stock.

quiz.q: What is a good incentive for a retailer to pay on time?
options: A) A 5% discount for payment within 7 days
B) A free trip to another country
C) A penalty for late payment
quiz.explanation: A small discount encourages timely payment and builds a good relationship.

quiz.q: Why should you book a market stall early?
options: A) To get a good location
quiz.explanation: Early booking ensures you get a visible spot with high foot traffic.

quiz.q: What should you have at your market stall to attract customers?
options: A) A bright cloth and clear price signs
quiz.explanation: Bright displays and clear prices make your stall inviting and easy to buy from.

quiz.q: What is a good market-day special offer?
quiz.explanation: A buy-5-get-1-free offer encourages larger purchases and attracts customers.

quiz.q: Why should you collect contact details at a trade fair?
options: A) To follow up with potential bulk buyers
D) To call them at night
quiz.explanation: Following up with interested contacts can lead to large orders.

quiz.q: What should you do after a market day to know if it was worth it?
options: A) Calculate your profit after covering stall fee and transport
quiz.explanation: Calculating profit helps you decide whether to participate again.

quiz.q: Why are schools good potential customers for tissues?
options: A) They use a lot of tissues daily
D) They are closed most of the year
quiz.explanation: Schools have many students and staff who use tissues regularly, creating steady demand.

quiz.q: What is the best way to approach a school for a tissue supply contract?
options: A) Give a free sample pack to the head teacher
C) Send a letter and never follow up
D) Offer a very high price
quiz.explanation: A free sample lets the school test your product before committing to a larger order.

quiz.q: Who in an office should you target to supply tissues?
options: A) The office manager or receptionist
quiz.explanation: The office manager or receptionist usually handles supplies and can make purchasing decisions.

quiz.q: What should you leave behind after giving a free sample to an office?
options: A) Your contact details and bulk price
quiz.explanation: Leaving your contact and bulk price makes it easy for them to order when ready.

quiz.q: How often should you follow up with a school or office after giving a sample?
options: A) Every two weeks until they order
quiz.explanation: Regular follow-up keeps you in their mind and shows you are serious about their business.

quiz.q: Why is word-of-mouth marketing powerful?
options: A) It is free and trusted by people
B) It costs a lot of money
C) It requires no product quality
D) It only works for big companies
quiz.explanation: People trust recommendations from friends and family, and it costs you nothing.

quiz.q: What should you do to encourage word-of-mouth?
options: A) Offer a reward for referrals
quiz.explanation: A small reward, like free packs, motivates customers to refer others.

quiz.q: What is a good way to use satisfied customers to advertise?
options: A) Ask them to post a photo on WhatsApp status
B) Ask them to keep quiet
D) Ask them to return the product
quiz.explanation: A photo on their status exposes your product to all their contacts for free.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer has a problem with your tissues?
quiz.explanation: Solving a problem quickly turns a dissatisfied customer into a loyal promoter.
